newsitem.title: UK: UK exporters to stay under knife of sharp sterling.
newsitem.headline: UK exporters to stay under knife of sharp sterling.

text.p: Heightened expectations for a boost in UK interest rates this week will keep shares of leading exporters under the knife edge of a strong sterling for the rest of the third quarter, strategists said.

Also second-tier industrials, a heavy component of the FTSE-250 index, should further underperform the market as their products become more expensive overseas and their profits are translated into fewer pounds back home.

On Tuesday, shares in steam and industrial fluid engineering compay Spirax-Sarco Engineering Plc, construction pipe systems maker Glynwed International Plc and specialist engineers IMI Plc all slid to their lowest levels in 12 months.
Lehman Brothers reduced its 1997 pre-tax profit estimates for IMI and tubing products maker TI Group Plc primarily due to sterling's strength.
Overall, the Mid-250 stocks have underperformed the lead index by 18 percent so far this year.
"I cannot believe that it is the beginning of the end yet for the manufacturing sector," said Edmund Shing, UK strategist at Schroders.

Some of Britain's best-known exporters, such as Imperial Chemical Industries Plc, TI Group Plc and British Steel Plc have reeled from the effects of the strong pound and analysts continue to slash profit estimates as sterling's strength persists.
Strategists say booming consumer demand, coupled with soaring sterling, has split the economy in two, and rising interest rates will simply make the distortion worse.
"I would think we would see more pain in the second half of the year in terms of company numbers and economic numbers," said Nigel Sedgley, an economist at Robert Fleming Securities.

The new Labour government's first budget last week initially knocked down industrial and chemical company shares, when investors realised that interest rates would have to go higher to cool off the red-hot consumer spending.

On Tuesday, sterling jumped to over six-year highs against the mark, after underlying retail prices unexpectedly rose to an annual 2.7 percent in June, overshooting the government's target of 2.5 percent.

The Bank of England is expected to raise official rates to at least 6.75 percent from 6.5 percent to keep the government's target in sight, after its two-day monetary policy committee meeting which starts on Wednesday.

A report from the Engineering Employers' Federation (EEF) said export orders among British engineering firms fell to the lowest level for three years in the second quarter, as sterling's noose around British exports tightened.
Still, strategists said share prices in these sterling-sensitive stocks had factored in a rate rise of 25 basis points.

What is perhaps more worrisome is that strategists are beginning to anticipate that a rate rise this week will be just the start of a series of future rate hikes throughout the year. A larger increase, followed by future monetary tightening, will hit exporters harder later this quarter, they said.
"We believe that there is a high probability for a 25 basis point hike and the market has pretty much discounted that," said Francois Langlade-Demoyen, European equities strategist at CSFB.
He expected further increases in base interest rates up to 7.25 percent.
"That means sterling is likely to get stronger and that will hit exporting companies further," he said.
